content.text: Chapter Two
Hunger in the Ashes

The mana wyrm struck at Falanaras’s wrist with all the spite of a hooked fish. He caught it behind the skull before its teeth found him, felt its narrow body twist through his grip, and drew a measured thread of power through the contact.

The creature shone blue-white beneath dark scales, its finned crest flattened and the long feelers beneath its jaw lashing at the chill air. The first pull tasted of rain striking metal. The second carried the thin sweetness of fruit left too long in sun. By the third, the tremor in his left hand eased. Falanaras stopped before relief could become pleasure and released the wyrm into the brass-ringed cage at his feet.

Captain Rynel Starweaver watched from the edge of the drill court. He wore no helmet, though the rest of the spellbreaker company had theirs on. Silver had entered the black of his hair since the war. His red-and-gold armor had been repaired so often that the plates no longer matched, yet he still stood inside it as if it had been forged around him. “Again,” he said.

Falanaras closed the cage and reached for his practice shield. Across the court, Theron Brightshield was trying to keep a second wyrm from winding its long feelers around his gauntlet. Lethira Valeflame leaned against the wall with her bow unstrung, laughing without sound while he swore at it. The laugh had become rarer since Silvermoon fell. Falanaras was glad to hear it, even at Theron’s expense.
“The point is to feed without fighting it,” Rynel told Theron. “If a wyrm has outmaneuvered you, it has learned more from the exercise than you have.”
Theron finally peeled the creature from his cuff. “Then it may apply for a commission.”
A few recruits smiled. Rynel did not, but the corner of his mouth relaxed before he turned to Falanaras. “Ward stance.”

Falanaras raised the shield. Rynel sent a narrow bolt of force at him. The spell hit the rim, slid along the etched runes, and burst against the paving stones in a shower of cold sparks without taking hold. Before the recoil left Falanaras’s shoulder, a brass practice ward unfolded beside Rynel and cast bands of blue force around Theron’s ankles. A second current hardened the ward’s thin legs against attack. Falanaras caught the binding on the hook of his glaive, peeled it from Theron, and laid it across the ward instead. In the same turn he stripped away the strengthening current and sent it around Theron’s armor, where blue light settled into the joints. The ward strained against its own restraint and tried to fire again. Falanaras found the command inside the conjuration, closed his will around that simpler purpose, and turned its crystal eye toward the straw target at the edge of the court. Its next bolt struck where he directed.

“Better,” the captain said. “You resisted what was meant to alter you. You moved completed workings instead of wasting strength making new ones. You took the ward because it is a made thing with a command simple enough to seize. Do not mistake that for command over a living caster.” He glanced at the caged wyrm. “And you drew before you began. That is the order. If feeding becomes the purpose rather than preparation, you become dangerous to the people behind you.”

No one mentioned the Wretched. They did not need to. The word occupied the court whenever a recruit held a wyrm too tightly or stared too long at the glow in another soldier’s palm. Rynel had begun every morning of the past month by making them feed under supervision. He claimed it was training. It was also inspection. He looked at their hands, their pupils, the tension around their mouths, and he remembered who had needed a second turn at the cages.

Before the Scourge, Falanaras had never imagined that a captain would need to know such things. Hunger had belonged to bad harvests, distant villages, and the poorer alleys of Murder Row. It had never belonged to Silvermoon itself. The Sunwell had filled the kingdom so completely that its abundance had passed unnoticed, as air did until it left the lungs.

Nor had the seasons seemed worthy of gratitude. Before the invasion, Eversong Woods had known only its enchanted spring: boughs green above the roads, blossom scent in the air, rain that came without winter’s teeth. When Arthas broke the runestone network, winter entered Quel’Thalas for the first time in living memory. Frost sealed the irrigation channels. Snow burdened roofs already split by siege, and survivors burned carved furniture to keep the refugee halls warm. The magisters restored enough of the runestones before the next winter to wake the old enchantment. Now undamaged groves flowered again while the Dead Scar kept its own chill. Falanaras noticed that recovered gentleness. Before the fall, he had mistaken it for permanence.

Rynel dismissed the company at midday with orders to report for city readiness duty. Falanaras retrieved his sword belt and found Lethira waiting beneath the cracked archway that led from the court. Her hair was braided tight for patrol, and a fresh scar ran beneath her left jaw. He had known her long enough to understand that asking after it would earn him a look sharp enough to draw blood.
“Your hand is steady,” she said instead.
“It was steady before.”

“Of course. And I have never missed a target.” She handed him a folded duty slate. “Feeding-house count at the Sunfury market, then a report from Murder Row. Rynel is sending the three of us because he finds our company soothing.”
Theron joined them with his helmet tucked under one arm. “He finds us expendable enough for a tedious assignment and competent enough to come back with a count.”
“That is the nearest he comes to affection,” Lethira said.

They crossed a city busy with the work of pretending it had survived intact. Masons floated pale blocks into the broken flank of a tower. Artificers knelt beside severed conduits, testing new ward-lines that glimmered briefly and failed. Merchants called from temporary stalls beneath silk awnings that hid scorched façades. Everywhere, workers had found uses for materials once saved for beauty: shattered crystal ground into mortar, brass railings hammered into braces, fragments of noble statuary stacked around open foundations.

At the market’s eastern end stood one of the new feeding houses. Its doors were copper, its windows clouded ward-glass, and two city guards kept the queue in a single line beneath the awning. Within, a fel crystal taller than a man burned green behind warded braces. Falanaras could not see its core clearly through the glass, only shadows stirring in the light and the slow pulse drawn out through silver conduits.

Those waiting did not speak of hunger. A woman in a mason’s apron asked the man behind her whether his hands had stopped cramping. An old clerk offered his place to a boy whose eyes had begun to unfocus. A young magister in red robes checked each token and wrote the time of every draw into a ledger. The language was orderly: maintenance, allotment, recovery. Everyone understood the other word waiting beneath it.

Falanaras had taken his first sanctioned draught of fel beneath such a roof. He remembered the shock more clearly than many things from that first year: fierce heat racing up his arm, the sensation of a locked door in his chest thrown wide, the immediate shame of wanting more. In the months that followed, green began to ring the blue of his irises, as it did in nearly everyone living among the city’s new crystals and wards. The healer had told him not to stare into the washbasin. Everyone did, eventually.

Small crystals still had their uses. The magisters recharged them before patrols, set them into field kits, and rationed them to sentries posted beyond the city. But a shard carried only a brief reserve, enough to steady a soldier until he reached a source or found a mana wyrm. The wyrms were everywhere now: tethered in markets, kept in barracks cages, carried by rangers in padded tubes. Rommath’s lesson had made them part of daily life. A blood elf who could not learn to tap a living current could not reliably serve beyond a warded street.

Rommath had returned again from Outland after Kael’thas departed, carrying methods learned in Illidan’s service and no patience for anyone who called them undignified. He had taught the magisters first, then soldiers, then wardens and labor crews. Find the current. Establish the hold. Draw only what was needed. Release before appetite became command. Falanaras had heard some older nobles call the practice degradation. He had seen most of them in the feeding-house line before the month was out.

Theron checked the house’s posted count, the guard roster, and the charge of the emergency shards secured behind the counter. Lethira questioned the handler tending a cluster of mana wyrms in a shaded pen. Falanaras copied the figures to the slate. It was dull work, which was why he noticed the silence gathering at the far end of the market.

A courier had stopped beside a public noticeboard. Dust whitened his boots to the knee. He held a packet bearing the regent’s seal, and the people near him watched with the fixed stillness of those who had taught themselves that news could only mean more names to mourn. An officer took the packet inside the market office. The courier mounted again without speaking. The crowd dispersed slowly, ashamed of having hoped for a message meant for them.
“No word from the prince,” Theron said quietly once they had moved on.
“There has not been for months,” Lethira replied. “That does not stop people from reading every sealed page as if he has remembered the road home.”

Falanaras understood the waiting, though he distrusted it. Kael’thas had returned after the Scourge withdrew, pale with exhaustion and still bearing the authority of a prince his people had needed desperately. He had gone with Rommath and Astalor Bloodsworn to the corrupted Sunwell and destroyed what Arthas had poisoned. The loss left every survivor reeling, yet few who had felt the necromancy inside that sacred current called the decision wrong. Then Kael’thas gathered them beneath broken banners, named them sin’dorei—the children of the blood—and promised that Quel’Thalas would endure.

The prince had kept moving after that. Stories reached Silvermoon in fragments: Garithos sending blood elf soldiers on missions meant to kill them, then condemning them when naga aid kept them alive; Kael’thas choosing Lady Vashj’s help over the judgment of men who had abandoned his people. Later came Illidan Stormrage, Outland, and the promise that somewhere beyond the world’s familiar borders there was power enough to answer what Quel’Thalas had lost. By the time Rommath returned with his grim practical knowledge, Kael’thas had been gone many months.
“The regent sends couriers,” Theron said. “The prince sends legends.”
Lethira glanced toward the market office. “One keeps roofs over people. The other lets them imagine a better roof someday.”

Their second assignment took them southwest toward Murder Row. Beyond the market, the rebuilt avenues narrowed and the repairs grew more provisional. Roofs sagged under patched tile. Shop windows were shuttered against daylight. Green light leaked beneath doors in thin, wavering bands. The feeding houses there were smaller, their ward-glass scratched and their guards paid enough to look away from certain transactions.

The route passed Dawnstar Terrace, where a relay housing stood open beneath a canvas awning. Rain from the previous night had found the gaps in unfinished paving and flooded the conduit trench. The old network had once hidden such workings beneath finished stone and effortless abundance. Now every repair exposed another dependency.

A work crew had gathered around the broken relay. The stone lay split open on the pavement, its interior runes blackened by damp. Two magisters stood knee-deep in a trench of runoff, arguing over a replacement conduit. A woman with plaster in her hair knelt beside a boy who was holding the end of a copper line above the water with both hands. His arms shook with the effort.
“That line should be grounded,” Theron said.
One of the magisters looked up, ready to take offense, then saw the spellbreaker insignia on Theron’s shoulder. “It was grounded. The lower contact failed.”
“And you have a child holding it over floodwater because?” Lethira asked.

“Because he is the only one here whose hands are small enough to reach behind the stone.” The magister said it defensively, then glanced at the boy and lowered his voice. “And because the wards on the western end will fail by nightfall if we do not reconnect it.”

Falanaras set down the duty slate and waded into the trench. Water soaked through his boots at once, cold enough to make his teeth ache. He took the copper line from the boy. A weak charge crawled through the metal into his palm—a loose current with nowhere to ground. He set his shield between the line and the flooded stone, caught the spill in the runes, and guided it away from the workers.
“Now,” he said.

The smaller magister reached into the fractured housing and fitted the contact home. For a moment nothing happened. Then the conduit flared with pale gold. The street lamps on the terrace kindled in a chain, one after another, their reflected light trembling across the water. A few people standing beneath nearby awnings applauded before remembering themselves.
The boy stared at Falanaras’s shield. “Did you take it from the line?”
“Only enough to keep it from taking you,” Falanaras said.

The answer seemed to matter to the child. He looked from the restored lamps to the magister, who had begun speaking rapidly about replacement housings and drainage stone. His mother caught his shoulder and drew him away from the trench. Before she left, she pressed two fingers to her brow in the old formal gesture of thanks. Her eyes were green at the edges. So were the boy’s.
Lethira waited until they were clear of the water. “You enjoyed that.”
“I enjoyed not watching a child get thrown through a wall.”
“You know what I mean.”

He did. Capturing a spell before it broke, feeling it pass through the shield’s runes and answer his hands, still carried a fierce clarity. Rynel’s warning returned: use the work after you feed. Do not feed for the feeling of work. Falanaras had followed the order. He knew that. Yet he could not deny the brief lift inside him when the lamps came alive.

Theron walked between them, carrying the soaked duty slate under his cloak. “Rynel would say that enjoying competence is permitted. He would then give a speech about the difference between competence and appetite.”
“A very long speech,” Lethira said.
“It would be concise,” Theron said. “We would simply have to listen to it repeatedly for the rest of our lives.”

They found the wardens outside an abandoned dye shop with weapons drawn toward the lane. A man in a torn clerk’s coat stood beneath a shuttered window, bent almost double. Green light crawled over his fingers. At his feet lay an overturned carrier cage and a mana wyrm that thrashed against the stones, its finned crest flared and its jaw-feelers snapping at empty air.
“How long?” Theron asked.
“He came out of the shop asking for a source,” one warden said. “Then he took the wyrm from a handler. He has already drained two lamp crystals.”

The man’s head lifted. Falanaras knew him then: a copyist named Varis, who had once sat at the district office’s outer desk with ink beneath his nails and a patient contempt for soldiers who misplaced their forms. The likeness had become difficult to hold. His face had drawn tight over his bones; his ears seemed too sharp for it, his mouth too pale and slack. Green fire leaked between the fingers he kept curled against his chest, but his eyes were a feverish, unfixed yellow.
“Varis,” Falanaras said. “Look at me. Release the wyrm.”

Varis answered with a sound that might once have been his name. Power tore through the lane. The wyrm’s blue-white light collapsed into his hand. He flung out his other arm, and the nearest ward-lamp guttered black. A second lamp failed across the street. Windows above them flashed as he reached for every loose thread of magic he could feel.

“Clear the houses,” Lethira said. Her first arrow struck the wall beside Varis’s shoulder, turning him away from the feeding house at the corner. Theron moved between the man and the wardens, shield raised. Falanaras caught the spill of stolen power in his own runes before it could lash back through the street.

Varis saw the restraint on the feeding house’s copper doors. He lunged for it. Theron met him shoulder-first. The impact drove them both into the lane, but Varis clawed at the shield rim, not trying to strike Theron so much as to pull through him toward the bound fire beyond the ward-glass.

Falanaras hooked Varis’s wrist with the rim of his own shield and forced the siphon away from the doors. The contact burned. For one instant he felt the frantic emptiness inside the other man: no thought of food, family, or pain, only the next current and the next and the next. It frightened him more than any blow.

Varis tore free with a strength his narrow body should not have held. He seized a warden’s field crystal from his belt and emptied it in a breath. The warden stumbled back, staring at the dead shard. Lethira’s second arrow cut Varis across the forearm. He did not seem to feel it.
“Pin him,” Theron said.

They moved together. Theron drove Varis backward with the shield. Lethira put an arrow through the sleeve of his coat and into the dye shop’s signpost, catching the fabric before he could reach another lamp. Falanaras stepped inside the arc of Varis’s flailing hands, struck the man behind the knee, and brought him down hard on the stones.

Varis bucked beneath them, dragging at the ward-lamps even as Theron bound his wrists. One lamp flickered. Falanaras planted his shield over the man’s hands and grounded the last of the siphon into the paving. The crackle faded. Varis went still so suddenly that Falanaras feared he had killed him.
Then Varis began to weep. He stared at the blood on his forearm, the dead field crystal, the exhausted wyrm curled in the gutter. Recognition returned in fragments, and terror arrived with it.
“Get a restraint wagon,” Falanaras told the wardens. “Take him to the district holding rooms. Put him under dampening wards before dark.”
One warden looked from Varis to the darkened lamps. “And if he turns again before the gate?”
Falanaras looked at Varis, who was weeping soundlessly into the stones. “Then you stop him. Do not make the street pay for your hesitation.”

Lethira retrieved the exhausted wyrm with a cloth and placed it gently in the carrier cage. “You will have to explain the lamps, the crystal, the arrow, and why you left him breathing,” Theron said as the wardens called for the wagon.

At the district office, they learned that the courier’s packet had carried revised allotment figures and nothing from Outland. The regent’s council had shifted two feeding-house crystals from the northern quarter to clinics near the western gates. The clerk delivering the news spoke in a careful, level voice. His fingers shook against the paper.
“Lor’themar is holding the city together with ledgers,” Lethira said once they were outside.
“Ledgers, patrols, and men who do not sleep,” Theron said.

Falanaras had seen the regent lord only twice since the fall, both times from the edge of a crowd. Lor’themar had none of Kael’thas’s brightness, none of the old royal distance that allowed strangers to place their hopes upon him. He looked like a ranger who had been handed too many reports and had resolved to read every one. It was a lesser kind of comfort, perhaps. It was still comfort.

They made their final report at dusk. Rynel listened without interrupting, one hand resting on the table in the barracks office. When Lethira reached the spent field crystal, he wrote an authorization for its replacement and pushed it toward the quartermaster.
Rynel folded his hands over the report. “The wardens will decide whether he can be confined. You gave them that choice instead of killing him in the lane. That is all.”
Lethira’s brow lifted. “You find us soothing after all.”
“I find you expensive,” Rynel said. “Go eat.”

Rynel kept Falanaras after the others had left the office. The barracks had settled into evening noise beyond the open door: bowls striking tables, boots on stairs, somebody attempting a song two rooms away and being told to stop. The captain turned the day’s report so that the lamp lit the columns of numbers. Feeding-house attendance. Wyrm losses. Restraint orders. Patrol requests. The pages looked harmless until Falanaras remembered Varis weeping in the gutter.
“Your draw this morning,” Rynel said. “How much?”
“Three measures.”
“And at the relay?”
“I redirected a spill. I did not feed from it.”
“Good.” Rynel did not look up from the report. “You wanted to.”
Falanaras felt the old instinct to deny it rise before he could stop it. The captain had not accused him. That made lying feel smaller. “For a moment.”

“Then you recognized it and did not.” Rynel marked something in the margin. “That is not failure. Do not make the mistake of believing the wish is proof that you are already lost. The mistake is making a home for it.”
Falanaras looked at the column headed CONDITION. Beside each name, Rynel had used the same clipped terms: stable, watch, restricted. No one in the company was marked unfit. Not yet.
“What is my condition?” he asked.
Rynel’s eyes lifted at last. “Capable of asking. Keep it that way.”

Later, Falanaras sat alone on the barracks steps while the last light drained from the repaired towers. In the distance, the Dead Scar remained a dark wound through the land, visible from the city’s higher streets when the weather was clear. It marked the road Arthas had cut north to Quel’Danas and followed south again when Quel’Thalas was finished. In the first months after the invasion, survivors and scattered messengers had learned that he reached Dalaran and destroyed that city as well. Each account differed in its details. None offered a reason to hope.

Caelir had been there when the war began. Falanaras had sent inquiries wherever a courier might carry them: to Dalaran’s surviving registries, to Alliance ports, to names in his brother’s old correspondence. At first he had written often, then less often, then only when a new list arrived. No answer had ever come. He had no grave to visit, no body to burn, no final witness who could tell him that Caelir had suffered or been spared. Absence became its own dull discipline.
Theron came out carrying three bowls of stew. He handed one over and sat beside him. Lethira followed with a cage containing a sleeping mana wyrm, its light a quiet blue between the bars.
“You are staring down the road again,” Theron said.
“I was thinking of Caelir.”
Neither of them offered him a false answer. That was one of the reasons he loved them.
After a time, Lethira said, “If he is alive, he will hear that Silvermoon still stands.”
Falanaras watched the blue glow of the wyrm. “He may not recognize what it has become.”
“Then he will have to learn,” Theron said. “We all did.”

Above them, the evening ward-lamps kindled one by one along the avenue. Their light was weaker than the old city radiance, uneven where the repairs had not yet met, but it reached across the stones. Falanaras ate his stew and felt the day’s measured draw settle inside him. The hunger remained. It would be there when he woke, and the wyrm cage would wait in the drill court, and someone in Murder Row would need more than the city could give.

Yet Silvermoon stood. Lor’themar held its daily burdens. Kael’thas remained somewhere beyond the sea, distant enough to become hope in the mouths of strangers. Rynel kept teaching soldiers to take what they needed and stop. For the moment, Falanaras could do the same. He set down the empty bowl, reached through the cage bars, and let the mana wyrm coil once around his fingers without drawing from it at all.
